title: How Many Cold Email Follow-Ups? A Sequence You Can Copy
summary: How many cold email follow-ups to send, how to space them, and what to say. Four example emails, a 5-step sequence table, and when to stop.
body_markdown:
A lot of cold email replies come from a follow-up, not the first email: one that lands on a quieter day, with a clearer angle. This post gives you a direct answer on how many follow-ups to send, how to space them, and a sequence you can copy today.


## How many follow-ups should you send?


A common range is **3 to 5 total touches** : the first email plus 2 to 4 follow-ups. Four or five is a sensible default if you're unsure.


Here's the trade-off at each end:


- **2 touches or fewer.** You leave replies on the table. Plenty of people mean to answer and simply forget, and a second or third nudge catches them.
- **3 to 5 touches.** Enough repetition to get noticed, with room for each email to say something different. This is where most small teams should start.
- **6 or more.** Each extra step tends to return fewer replies and more "please stop" responses and unsubscribes. Spam complaints hurt every future send from that domain, so the cost isn't just one annoyed prospect.


The real limit isn't a number. It's whether you have something new to say. If your fourth email is "just bumping this," you've already run out of material, and you should stop at three.


## How far apart should follow-ups be?


A common starting point is to **widen the gaps as you go** : 2 to 3 days after the first email, then 3 to 4 days, then about a week.


Short gaps early keep you in context while the first email is still in their inbox. Longer gaps later stop you from feeling relentless. A full 5-step sequence usually spans 2 to 3 weeks.


Two practical rules:


- **Send on business days only** , in the prospect's time zone, during their working hours. A send window handles this for you.
- **Don't send every step at the same hour.** If the first email went at 9am Tuesday, try the next one mid-afternoon on a Thursday. Different moments catch different inbox habits.


## Same thread or new thread?


**Default to the same thread** (reply to your own email, keep the "Re:" subject) for the first one or two follow-ups. The prospect sees the original context right below, and you don't need to re-explain yourself.


**Start a new thread** when you're switching angles hard, like moving from a pain-point pitch to a case for a different use case, or when the original subject line clearly didn't land. A fresh subject gets a fresh look in the inbox.


A simple pattern that works for many teams: steps 1 to 3 in one thread, step 4 as a new thread with a new subject, step 5 back as a short reply to step 4.


## What each follow-up should do


Every follow-up needs a job. If you can't name the job, cut the step.


Job What it does Keep it to


**New angle** Pitches a different problem or benefit than email 1 3 to 5 sentences


**Proof** Shows a result, a specific example, or how a similar team uses it 3 to 4 sentences


**Simple question** Asks one easy yes/no or "who should I ask" question 1 to 2 sentences


**Breakup** Closes the loop politely and leaves the door open 2 to 3 sentences


Notice what's missing: "just checking in," "bumping this to the top of your inbox," and "did you see my last email?" Those give the reader nothing new to respond to.


## 4 example follow-up emails


These assume your first email pitched a tool that helps finance teams close the books faster. Swap in your own product and details. The` {{firstName}}` and` {{company}}` tags are personalization variables.


### Follow-up 1: new angle (same thread, day 3)


> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> One more thought. Beyond the month-end close, most teams we talk to lose the most time on vendor reconciliations in the middle of the month.
>
>
> If that's a pain at {{company}}, I can show you how we'd cut it down in 15 minutes.
>
>
> Worth a look?


### Follow-up 2: proof (same thread, day 7)


> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> Quick example: a 6-person finance team moved their reconciliations into our tool and stopped doing them in spreadsheets. Their controller said the biggest win was not chasing missing receipts at the end of the month.
>
>
> Happy to send a 2-minute walkthrough if useful.


Only use proof you can actually back up. A real, specific example from a customer (with permission) beats a vague "companies like yours see great results." If you don't have one yet, describe exactly how the product works for a team like theirs instead.


### Follow-up 3: simple question (new thread, day 12)


Subject: *who owns reconciliations at {{company}}?*


> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> Are you the right person for questions about month-end reconciliations, or is there someone else I should reach out to?


Short questions are easy to answer from a phone. Even a "not me, talk to Dana" reply is progress.


### Follow-up 4: breakup (reply to step 3, day 19)


> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> I'll stop reaching out here. If faster reconciliations become a priority later, just reply to this email and I'll pick it back up.
>
>
> Thanks either way.


A good breakup email isn't a guilt trip. Skip "I guess you're not interested." Keep it polite so they feel comfortable coming back in three months.


## An example 5-step email-only sequence


Here's the full sequence in one view, a reasonable default for founders and SDRs starting out.


Step Day Thread Job Length


1 Day 1 New First email: one clear problem, one ask 50 to 120 words


2 Day 3 Same thread New angle 40 to 80 words


3 Day 7 Same thread Proof 40 to 80 words


4 Day 12 New thread, new subject Simple question Under 30 words


5 Day 19 Reply to step 4 Breakup Under 40 words

## Swapping 1 to 2 steps for LinkedIn


If your prospects are active on LinkedIn, replacing one or two email steps with LinkedIn touches gives them a second place to notice you.


Here's the sequence above with the new-angle and simple-question emails moved to LinkedIn:


Step Day Channel Action


1 Day 1 Email First email


2 Day 2 LinkedIn Profile visit


3 Day 3 LinkedIn Connection request, no note or a one-line note


4 Day 7 Email Proof follow-up (same thread)


5 After connected LinkedIn Short message: the simple question


6 Day 19 Email Breakup


A profile visit and a connection request are light touches, and the message only goes out if they accept.


A few cautions. LinkedIn doesn't publish its exact limits, so keep daily actions conservative. LinkedIn's terms also restrict automation, so use automation knowingly and accept that risk. Our post on[LinkedIn automation limits](https://supersend.io/blog/linkedin-automation-limits) covers safe pacing, and[running cold email and LinkedIn in one sequence](https://supersend.io/blog/cold-email-and-linkedin-sequence) goes deeper on mixed sequences.


## When to stop


Stopping at the right time matters as much as following up. Set these rules before you launch:


- **A reply on any channel stops everything.** If they reply on LinkedIn, the next email must not go out. In SuperSend, a reply on either channel stops both.
- **Unsubscribes and "please remove me" stop immediately** , and that contact goes on your do-not-contact list for good. Honor these fast, even when they're phrased informally.
- **Out-of-office replies pause, not stop.** An auto-reply isn't a real response. Note the return date, pause the contact, and resume the sequence a day or two after they're back. If the OOO names a colleague to contact instead, that's worth a separate, personal email.
- **Bounces stop and get flagged.** A bounce means the address is bad. Remove it and check your list source if you see more than a handful.


## A/B testing your follow-ups


Once the sequence is running, test it. The rule is **change one variable at a time** , or you won't know what caused the difference.


Good things to test, in roughly this order:


1. **The subject line of step 1** (it decides whether anything else gets read)
2. **The angle of the first follow-up** (pain point A vs pain point B)
3. **The call to action** (a meeting ask vs "worth a look?")
4. **Spacing** (day 3 vs day 5 for the first follow-up)


Give each variant enough sends before calling a winner. A common rule of thumb is a few hundred sends per variant at minimum, and judge on replies, not opens. Open tracking is unreliable because many email clients load images automatically or block them.


## The short version


- Send **3 to 5 total touches** . Stop sooner if you run out of genuinely new things to say.
- Space them out with **widening gaps** : about day 3, day 7, day 12, day 19.
- Keep early follow-ups in the **same thread** , and use a **new thread** when you change angle.
- Give each step a job: **new angle, proof, simple question, breakup** . Swap 1 to 2 steps for LinkedIn if your buyers live there.
- **Stop on any reply** on any channel, honor unsubscribes immediately, pause for out-of-office, and A/B test **one variable at a time** .
